questions.question: What does integration by parts do to a product inside an integral?
options: It rewrites every integral as a limit of a sequence.
It transfers derivatives between two functions inside an integral.
It applies only to integrals of constant functions.
It replaces every product by a quotient.

questions.question: Which formula matches the indefinite integration by parts rule?
Using integration by parts with $f(x) = x$ and $g'(x) = \mathrm e^x$, which expression is obtained for $\int x\mathrm e^x\,\mathrm{d}x$ before simplifying the remaining integral?
For $\int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$, which boundary term appears in the definite integration by parts formula?
Which prerequisite rule is integration by parts based?
options: The definition of a singleton set.
The rule for adding endpoints of intervals.

questions.question: In the definite formula, which condition is required for the derivatives $f'$ and $g'$?
options: They must both be strictly increasing.
They must both vanish at the endpoints.

questions.question: Let $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = \ln x$ on $[1,2]$. Which term is subtracted in integration by parts for $\int_1^2 x^2\,\mathrm{d}(\ln x)$?
Using integration by parts, which expression is correct for $\int_0^1 x\,\mathrm{d}x$ if $f(x) = x$ and $g'(x) = 1$?
Why is the choice of functions in integration by parts important?
options: Because the formula is valid only when $f = g$.
Because one must always choose the larger function as $f$.
Because the formula removes all boundary terms only for one choice.
Because moving the derivative must simplify the remaining integral

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relation between definite and indefinite integration by parts?
options: The method applies only to definite integrals.
The method applies only to indefinite integrals.
It applies to both; boundary terms appear in the definite case
The definite version has no remaining integral.

questions.question: Let $f$ and $g$ satisfy the assumptions on $[a,b]$, and suppose $g$ is constant. What does integration by parts imply about $\int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
For $\int_0^1 x^2\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x$, why is integration by parts a natural method?
options: It is a product integral, which the technique handles
It is an integral over an empty interval.
It has no functions whose derivatives can be discussed.
It is solved by changing every endpoint into $0$.

questions.question: What rule is integration by parts derived from?
What does integration by parts transfer inside an integral?
options: A derivative from one factor to another
A set operation into a limit

questions.question: Which type of integrals can integration by parts be applied to?
Using $u=x$ and $\mathrm{d}v=\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x$, what is $\int x\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x$ transformed into?
In $\int f\,\mathrm{d}g=fg-\int g\,\mathrm{d}f$, what term appears before the remaining integral?
For $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, what is the boundary term $f(1)g(1)-f(0)g(0)$?
Why is the choice of $f$ and $g$ important in integration by parts?
options: Any choice always gives the same difficulty
The choice changes the definition of derivative
A good choice makes the remaining integral simpler
The choice removes the boundary term
